The word intransitive is an adjective that means: not passing across to something else; not transferring to an object.

The prefix "in-" simply means "not," and "transitive" comes from the idea of something passing over or transferring. So intransitive = not passing over, not transferring. The action stays put. It doesn't reach out and land on anything else.

This word has its main home in grammar, and a secondary use in mathematics. Both uses share the exact same underlying idea, just applied to different things.

This is where you'll encounter "intransitive" most often — describing a type of verb.

When a verb is intransitive, it means the action is complete all by itself. The action begins with the subject and ends there. It doesn't need to land on, or be "received by," a separate person or thing (called a "direct object") to make sense.

Consider these sentences:

  • She sleeps.
  • The baby cried.
  • He arrived.
  • The bird flew.
  • She sneezed.

Every one of these is perfectly complete. You don't need to add anything. There's no receiver of the action. "She sleeps" — sleeps what? That question doesn't even make sense. "He arrived" — arrived what? Again, nonsense. The action simply happens, fully contained within the subject.

These verbs — sleep, cry, arrive, fly, sneeze — are intransitive.

Contrast: Transitive Verbs

To truly lock in "intransitive," you need to understand what it's being contrasted with: a transitive verb.

A transitive verb is one where the action does pass across to something — it needs a direct object to be complete, or at least makes clear sense with one.

  • She kicked _? → the ball. ✓ The action lands on the ball.
  • He read _? → a book. ✓ The action lands on the book.
  • They built _? → a house. ✓ The action lands on the house.

With transitive verbs, the action "travels across" from the subject to the object. Something receives the action.

Think of it like throwing a ball. A transitive verb is a throw that lands somewhere — there's a catcher (the object). An intransitive verb is a wave of the hand — it just happens, and nothing catches it.

The Simple Test

Whenever you want to know if a verb is being used intransitively, ask: "[verb] what?" or "[verb] whom?"

  • "She sneezed" — sneezed what? → Makes no sense. Intransitive.
  • "He kicked" — kicked what? → Makes sense; you'd expect an answer. Transitive.

If the question makes no sense or has no answer in the sentence, the verb is intransitive.

The Same Verb Can Be Both

This is important and often surprises learners: many verbs can be transitive in one sentence and intransitive in another. The verb itself isn't permanently one or the other — it depends on how it's used.

  • She runs the company. — runs what? The company. Transitive.
  • She runs every morning. — runs what? Nothing. She just runs. Intransitive.
  • He ate the pizza. — ate what? The pizza. Transitive.
  • He ate slowly. — ate what? Nothing stated. Intransitive.
  • The chef cooked a meal. — Transitive.
  • The chef cooked for hours. — Intransitive.

This is why dictionaries often mark a verb's individual definitions as either transitive or intransitive — because the same word can function both ways.

When you look a verb up in a dictionary and see labels like vt (verb transitive) or vi (verb intransitive), or the abbreviations tr. and intr., that's exactly this distinction being marked for you.

Why Does It Matter?

Understanding whether a verb is intransitive helps you build correct, natural sentences. If a verb is intransitive, you cannot put a direct object after it without it sounding wrong.

You'd never say: "She slept the bed" or "He arrived the station." Those sound wrong precisely because sleep and arrive are intransitive — they can't take a direct object.

You can, however, add other kinds of information (like time, place, or manner) after an intransitive verb:

  • She slept for eight hours.
  • He arrived at the station.

"For eight hours" and "at the station" are not direct objects — they're extra descriptive information. That's perfectly fine with intransitive verbs.
In Mathematics and Logic: Intransitive Relations

The same adjective appears in math and logic to describe a certain kind of relationship — and the core meaning is identical: the relationship does not carry forward through a chain.

First, a transitive relation (so you can contrast): "is taller than" is transitive. If Alice is taller than Bob, and Bob is taller than Carol, then Alice must be taller than Carol. The relationship carries all the way through the chain.

An intransitive relation breaks that chain. "Is the mother of" is a classic example. If Alice is the mother of Bob, and Bob is the mother of Carol, then Alice is absolutely not the mother of Carol — she's the grandmother. The "mother of" relationship does not pass through. It stops. It doesn't transfer to the next link in the chain.

Another example: "is the next number after." 3 is the next number after 2, and 4 is the next number after 3 — but 4 is certainly not "the next number after" 2. The relationship doesn't carry through.

No matter where you see the word "intransitive" — grammar or math — it always means the same thing at its heart:

The action, effect, or relationship does not pass across to something beyond itself. It does not transfer. It stays contained.

In grammar: the verb's action stays with the subject; it doesn't pass across to a direct object.
In math: the relationship between two things doesn't automatically carry forward to a third thing.

Once you see that single through-line, the word "intransitive" will always make sense to you, wherever you encounter it.
